content.page: Extract from clinical guideline on imaging and biomarkers in acute pulmonary embolism
content.summary: Echocardiography and computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA) are used to assess right ventricular (RV) morphology and function for prognostic stratification in acute pulmonary embolism (PE). Echocardiographic RV dysfunction is common (~25% of unselected acute PE patients) and is associated with increased short-term mortality but has low positive predictive value for PE-related death in some meta-analyses. CTPA-derived RV enlargement and increased RV/LV ratio are reproducibly associated with worse outcomes.

echocardiography_findings.prevalence: Approximately 25% of unselected patients with acute PE have RV dysfunction on echocardiography.
echocardiography_findings.prognostic_value: Systematic reviews/meta-analyses suggest echocardiographic RV dysfunction is associated with elevated short-term mortality in haemodynamically stable patients, but overall positive predictive value for PE-related death is low (<10%) in at least one meta-analysis.
echocardiography_findings.additional_findings: Echocardiography can identify right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale (PFO) and right heart thrombi; both findings are associated with increased mortality. PFO also increases risk of ischaemic stroke from paradoxical embolism in patients with PE and RV dysfunction.

ctpa_section_5.2.2.note: CTPA parameters used for early risk stratification are summarized in supplementary data (Table 3).
ctpa_section_5.2.2.what_ct_detects: Four-chamber CT views can detect RV enlargement (RV end-diastolic diameter and RV/LV ratio measured in transverse or four-chamber view) as an indicator of RV dysfunction.

supporting_evidence.finding: RV enlargement (defined by RV/LV ratio threshold noted in study) was an independent predictor of adverse in-hospital outcome; reported hazard ratios in the study indicate substantially increased risk (examples: HR ~3.5 overall; HR ~3.8 in haemodynamically stable patients).

An increased RV/LV ratio >1.0 on CT was associated with ~2.5-fold increased risk for all-cause mortality (OR ~2.5, 95% CI ~1.8–3.5) and ~5-fold risk for PE-related mortality (OR ~5.0, 95% CI ~2.7–9.2).

thresholds_and_interpretation.mild_dilation: Mild RV dilation (RV/LV slightly above 0.9) is frequent (>50% of haemodynamically stable PE patients) but probably has minor prognostic significance.
thresholds_and_interpretation.recommended_threshold: RV/LV ratios ≥1.0 (instead of 0.9) on CT angiography may be more appropriate to indicate poor prognosis, as larger ratios associate with rising prognostic specificity.

ctpa_section_5.2.2.additional_ct_metrics: Volumetric analysis of heart chambers and assessment of contrast reflux into the inferior vena cava (IVC) may provide further prognostic information.

prognostic_implications.overall: Both echocardiography and CTPA provide valuable prognostic information in normotensive patients with acute PE, with CTPA-derived RV/LV ratio being a widely reported predictor of adverse outcome.
prognostic_implications.limitations: Echocardiographic parameters have proved difficult to standardize; some measures have limited positive predictive value for PE-related death.

content.references_mentioned: Multiple references cited throughout (numerical citations present) supporting statements, including systematic reviews, meta-analyses, prospective cohorts, and supplementary tables.
